newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo oil spill - Who foots the bill?.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo oil spill - Who foots the bill?.

text.p: Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd, which owns the estimated 13,400 tonnes of oil scattered across large sections of Tokyo Bay, may be largely sheltered from the liability related to the spill's cleanup costs, analysts and officials said on Wednesday.

But Japan's largest shipping company, Nippon Yusen KK, whose subsidiary is the owner and operator of the supertanker Diamond Grace, which spilled the oil, may face considerable damages, officials say, depending on the size of the cleanup cost.

The 259,999 deadweight tonne vessel, which was carrying some 1.5 million barrels of crude oil from the Middle East to a refinery in Kawasaki, on the southern outskirts of Tokyo, scraped a reef in shallow waters of Tokyo Bay and had released some 100,000 barrels of crude oil by mid-afternoon.

The incident follows another major spill that hit Japan in January, when the breakup of the Russian tanker Nakhodka spread 5,200 tonnes (about 36,400 barrels) of heavy fuel oil along a wide section of the Sea of Japan coast. Latest estimates put the cost of that spill at 36 billion yen ($316 million).
According to the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), for vessels over 140,000 gross tonnes, shipowners are covered by international oil spill damage establishments for up to $194 million.
The coverage comes from an initial $85.9 million allotment from the Civil Liability Convention, established by the IMO in 1969 and amended in a 1992 protocol.

The additional $109.9 million comes from the Fund Convention, or officially, the International Convention on the Establishment of an International Fund for Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage, essentially a slush fund set up in 1971 and updated in 1992 by major oil importing countries, in order to share oil pollution costs.
The terms of the international agreement for oil pollution damages divide the burden of payment between the member countries according to the volume of each country's crude imports.
After damages exceed the $194 million, the shipowner bears the primary burden of liability, depending on the arrangement between the owner of the oil and the shipping company.

"If you charter a ship on a spot basis, it's like hailing a taxi -- all or most of the liability is on the driver, the shipowner," said Mark Jenkin, who heads research for global tanker broker Simpson, Spence, and Young.

"If you time charter a vessel, it's more like hiring or renting a car -- you've got to bring it back in good shape, but if you sign the right papers and pay a small amount, damages can still lie with the rental company," he added.
Maritime insurance specialists say are further covered by individual coverage they hold.

"Most shipowners protect themselves from such eventualities by taking part in protection and indemnity clubs (P&I), of which there are about 16 major clubs in the world," said Justin Gardner, a London-based shipping insurance analyst.
He said: "For oil pollution, these clubs cover them for up to $500 million, and shipowners have the option to increase that coverage." ($1=114 yen)
